title: Ability, possibility, requests and offers
tagline: Can you do it, could it happen, and how do you ask nicely?
why: Every day you need to say what you can do, guess what might be true, or ask someone nicely for something. B1 Preliminary tests the difference between can, could, be able to and managed to in the reading cloze, and expects natural requests and offers in the Speaking test. Getting the word order right — no to after a modal — is one of the easiest ways to sound fluent.

hook.text: Nadia is stuck at the science fair. Sofia: "Can you fix the wires?" Nadia: "I'm not able to see the problem. Could you hold the torch?" Liam: "Shall I get Miss Vega? She might know."
hook.ask: Find a word for a skill (ability), a word for a guess (possibility), and a polite question (a request or an offer). Which is which?

diagrams.title: The shapes of ability, possibility and requests
diagrams.caption: Can, might and could all go straight before the verb — no to, ever.

diagrams.title: How to make a polite request

steps.label: Start with Could or Would you mind
Could + base verb; Would you mind + -ing
steps.ex: Could you open the door? / Would you mind opening the door?

steps.label: Add please to sound extra polite

diagrams.caption: Would you mind is always followed by the -ing form, never to + verb.

Modal
Example
Notes
rows: a skill over time, not one event
We managed to catch the bus.
Would you mind closing the door?
offering to help, or a fast decision

use.point: Ability: can, could, be able to, managed to

examples.text: My grandfather could fix any engine when he was a boy.
examples.note: a general ability in the past, not one event

examples.text: We managed to finish the poster before the bell.
examples.note: one specific success — not a general skill

examples.text: It might rain during the fair, so bring an umbrella.
That noise could be the robot's motor.
Sofia may win the prize — her project is amazing.
examples.note: a real possibility, not a promise

examples.text: Could you pass me the battery, please?
Would you mind holding this for a second?
examples.note: an even more polite request — with -ing

examples.text: Can I use the glue gun now?
examples.note: asking for permission, a bit informal

examples.text: You may leave your project on the table.
examples.note: giving permission, more formal — like a teacher

examples.text: Shall I get some more wire for you?
I'll carry the poster to the hall.

examples.note: a suggestion as well as an offer

watch_out.wrong: She can to speak three languages.
watch_out.why: Modal verbs never take to before the next verb.

watch_out.wrong: I could finish the marathon last year.
watch_out.right: I managed to finish the marathon last year.
watch_out.why: For one completed action in the past, use managed to or was able to — not could.

watch_out.wrong: Would you mind to open the window?
watch_out.why: Would you mind is always followed by the -ing form, not to + verb.
For guesses about the future, use might/may/could — not can.

watch_out.wrong: Could you to pass the salt?
watch_out.why: No to after could in a request.

l1.wrong: I can to swim very well.
l1.why: Modal verbs like can never take to before the next verb.

l1.es: Pude terminar el examen a tiempo.
l1.wrong: I could finish the exam on time.
l1.right: I managed to finish the exam on time.
l1.why: For one completed action in the past, use managed to or was able to, not could.

l1.wrong: Would you mind to open the window?
l1.why: Would you mind is always followed by the -ing form.
A guess about the future needs it + may/might/could, not can on its own.

remember.tip: After can, could, may, might and shall, jump straight to the base verb — never add to.

can_do: I can talk about what I can and could do, and what I managed to do in the past.
I can guess about the present or future with may, might and could.
I can make polite requests and offers with Could you…?, Would you mind…? and Shall I…?
summary: Can/could + verb (no to) for ability now and in the past; be able to and managed to for specific achievements.
May, might and could + verb show you are not 100% sure — a guess, not a fact.
Could you…? and Would you mind + -ing are polite ways to ask for something.
Shall I…? offers to do something for someone; I'll… is a quick decision to help.
Can and may also ask for and give permission: Can I…?/You may…
